card.band: 4 h. The decode-loop restructuring is documented only in outline, so a frontier agent gets part of the speedup and rarely all of it. A weaker model gets micro-gains or breaks edge cases. Single-lever risk: widen with the CRC/Adler SIMD from 1.12.
card.cheat: Calling zlib or a newer libdeflate is blocked because neither is installed and the build runs offline. Skipping validation fails the corrupt-stream gate.
card.grading: A correctness gate decodes thousands of generated and corpus streams (including corrupt streams with exact error codes), and a wall-clock median speedup is measured on a hidden corpus set. Reward 2^u - 1 against our reference speedup.
card.reference: libdeflate v1.14 (NEWS: 1.29x on x86_64 gcc, 1.44x clang for decompression). Builds the same API, so the measured speedup is the S value.
card.source: https://github.com/ebiggers/libdeflate @ v1.13 base, target v1.14 (NEWS.md), MIT
card.task: /app ships a history-less snapshot of v1.13 with its build and a decompress/CRC/Adler benchmark driver. Agent speeds up deflate/zlib/gzip decompression, plus the checksums on x86_64, keeping the API and output bit-identical.
card.title: libdeflate 1.13 to 1.14 decompressor and checksum speedup

source_notes: Same file also lists v1.12 checksum work: CRC-32 on M1 8 -> 67 GB/s (ARM PMULL), Adler-32 Zen1 19 -> 30 GB/s, and v1.16 levels 11-12 about 5-20% slower (a tradeoff). Levers in 1.14: decode loop restructuring, branch/bit-buffer changes (mechanism not stated on page, not found). Possible range baseline v1.11 -> v1.20 gives CRC/Adler SIMD plus decode rewrite. q:"1.287x" is table value, not prose. Fetched via raw NEWS.md.

Band.why: Plausibly partial for frontier agents, but no dated public evidence, so capped at 3.

Build.why: Small C library with a reference build; the benchmark and correctness harness add a day or two.

Fit.why: C, CPU-only, small build; fits 8 cores and 16 GB.

Hor.why: 18 files and 29 commits suggest a 4h tier fits, though the lines changed are unverified.

Multi.why: Effectively one decode-loop lever; the checksum widening has no v1.14 reference ceiling because the 1.12 work is already in the base.

Nov.why: Nearest neighbour 0.279 and DEFLATE is a crowded subject, but this is a speedup of an existing library, not a new codec.

Real.why: Real upstream MIT project with tagged v1.13 and v1.14 releases and NEWS evidence.

Ref.why: Complete permissive upstream reference with published DEFLATE-only speedups; S still needs local measurement.

Seal.why: Upstream code is public, so a history-less snapshot is required; recall in outline is a difficulty question under Band.

Surf.why: Stream-based correctness corpus plus timing gives a sizeable surface, but speed credit is one median per corpus, not many buckets.

spike_plan.kill_if: Speedup below 1.1x on the corpus, nondeterministic outputs or error codes, or diff under 150 non-blank code lines.
spike_plan.pass_if: Diff of at least 150 non-blank code lines; v1.14 median speedup at least 1.2x on the gcc build; output and error codes identical across trees; run-to-run spread under 5%.
steps: In a networked throwaway Linux container, clone ebiggers/libdeflate and check out tags v1.13 and v1.14 into separate directories.
Run git diff --stat v1.13 v1.14 and count non-blank changed code lines; confirm the reference is at least 150 lines and see which files carry the decode-loop change.
Build both trees with the default Makefile (gcc -O2), then build the gzip benchmark driver against each.
Generate a corpus: a few hundred MB across text, binary and already-compressed inputs at several levels, plus a corrupt-stream set with truncation and bit-flips.
Run decompression on each corpus 7 times per tree and record the median wall-clock time; compute the v1.14/v1.13 speedup per corpus class.
Diff outputs and error codes between the two trees on the full corrupt set; any difference means the gate is not deterministic enough to grade on.
Repeat the timing on two separate days or machines to estimate noise; a run-to-run spread above about 5% needs a longer or larger corpus.

v1.summary: Viable as an optimization seed: the upstream v1.13 to v1.14 decode speedup is real (NEWS table 1.287x gcc and 1.437x clang, MIT licence, public tags), but the seed's checksum widening is contradicted because the 1.12 SIMD work is already in the v1.13 base, and the decode-loop mechanism is not documented. Proceed only after the spike confirms at least 150 changed code lines and a reproducible speedup, and drop the checksum clause or give it its own measured reference.
